title: Quadrilaterals
subject: Maths-1
description: Grade 8 practice on rectangles, squares, parallelograms, rhombuses, kites and trapeziums — their definitions, diagonal properties, angle facts and the congruence proofs behind them.

questions.question: The word 'quadrilateral' comes from two Latin words. What do 'quadri' and 'latus' mean?
options: four and side
four and angle
square and side
corner and line
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that 'quadri' means four and 'latus' refers to sides — a quadrilateral is a four-sided figure.

questions.question: What is the sum of all the angles of any quadrilateral?
questions.explanation: Drawing one diagonal splits any quadrilateral into two triangles, each with angle sum 180°, so the total is 2 × 180° = 360°.

questions.question: How does the chapter prove that the angles of quadrilateral SOME add up to 360°?
options: Measure the four angles of several quadrilaterals and add the results up
Extend each side to form exterior angles that together make 360°
Draw diagonal SM to split it into two triangles, each with angle sum 180°
Draw both diagonals to split it into four triangles, each with angle sum 180°
questions.explanation: Diagonal SM creates ΔSEM and ΔSOM. Their six angles total 180° + 180° = 360°, and regrouping them gives exactly the four angles of the quadrilateral. Four triangles from two diagonals would give 720° and need the central angles subtracted.

questions.question: The angles of a quadrilateral are 70°, 110° and 85°. What is the fourth angle?
questions.explanation: 70 + 110 + 85 = 265, and 360 − 265 = 95°. Picking 85° repeats a given angle; 105° comes from subtracting from 370.

questions.question: It is possible to construct a quadrilateral with three right angles and a fourth angle of 100°.
questions.explanation: Three right angles already use 270°, so the fourth angle must be 360° − 270° = 90°. A fourth angle of 100° would make the total 370°, which is impossible.

questions.question: In exercise Q10 one vertex of quadrilateral ABCD is pushed inward so the shape is 'dented'. What happens to its angle sum?
options: Still 360°, since joining BD still gives two triangles
Less than 360°, because one angle folds inwards
More than 360°, because one angle exceeds 180°
Exactly 180°, since it becomes one big triangle
questions.explanation: The answer key joins BD: ΔADB and ΔBDC each have angle sum 180°, so the dented quadrilateral still totals 360°. The inward (reflex) angle is simply larger than 180°, but the total does not change.

questions.question: The angles of a quadrilateral are x, 2x, 3x and 4x. What is x?
questions.explanation: x + 2x + 3x + 4x = 10x = 360°, so x = 36°. Using 180° (a triangle's sum) would wrongly give 18°; 40° would make the total 400°.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements that are true about angle sums.
options: Every quadrilateral's angles add up to 360°
Every triangle's angles add up to 180°
A quadrilateral's angles add up to 180°
A quadrilateral can have four angles of 100° each
A quadrilateral's angle sum depends on its side lengths
questions.explanation: A triangle totals 180° and a quadrilateral (two triangles) totals 360°, regardless of side lengths. Four angles of 100° would total 400°, which is impossible.

questions.question: A quadrilateral in which all four angles are equal must have each angle equal to 90°, so it is a rectangle.
questions.explanation: Four equal angles share 360°, so each is 360° ÷ 4 = 90°. A quadrilateral with all angles 90° is a rectangle by the chapter's definition (exercise Q11(vi) is True).

questions.topic: Rectangle Definitions and the Carpenter's Problem
questions.question: What is the FIRST definition of a rectangle given in the chapter?
options: Opposite sides are parallel and also equal
Diagonals are equal and perpendicular
All angles are 90° and opposite sides are equal
All angles are 90° and all sides are equal
questions.explanation: The opening definition states two conditions: all angles are right angles and opposite sides have equal length. 'All sides equal' describes a square; 'parallel and equal' describes a parallelogram.

questions.topic: Rectangle Definitions and the Carpenter's Problem
questions.question: The carpenter already has one 8 cm strip. How long should the other strip be to form a rectangle?
options: 4 cm
16 cm
6 cm
8 cm
questions.explanation: Deduction 1 shows the diagonals of a rectangle are always equal, so the second strip must also be 8 cm. 4 cm is the half-diagonal, not the full strip.

questions.topic: Rectangle Definitions and the Carpenter's Problem
questions.question: Where should the two strips be joined so that the thread through their ends forms a rectangle?
options: At their midpoints
At their endpoints
At one-third of their length
At any point on each strip
questions.explanation: Deduction 2 proves the diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other, so each strip must be crossed at its midpoint — the strips must be equal AND joined at their midpoints.

questions.topic: Rectangle Definitions and the Carpenter's Problem
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the chapter's equivalent definitions of a rectangle?
options: A quadrilateral with all angles 90° and opposite sides equal
A quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel and equal
A quadrilateral in which all the angles are 90°
A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other
questions.explanation: Opposite sides parallel and equal only guarantees a parallelogram (exercise Q5 answers 'No'). The other three are all shown in the chapter to capture exactly the rectangles.

questions.topic: Rectangle Definitions and the Carpenter's Problem
questions.question: Why can the definition of a rectangle be shortened to just 'all angles are 90°'?
options: Because a quadrilateral with equal opposite sides always has 90° angles
Because the diagonal definition makes the side lengths completely irrelevant
Because all angles being 90° already forces the opposite sides to be equal
Because the sides of any quadrilateral are always equal in opposite pairs
questions.explanation: Deduction 4 joins diagonal BD and proves ΔBAD ≅ ΔDCB (AAS), so AD = CB and DC = BA. Hence 'opposite sides equal' need not be stated separately.

questions.topic: Rectangle Definitions and the Carpenter's Problem
questions.question: The chapter gives a definition of a rectangle that uses only its diagonals: they are equal and bisect each other.
questions.explanation: After the Carpenter's Problem the chapter states: 'A rectangle is a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other.'

questions.topic: Rectangle Definitions and the Carpenter's Problem
questions.question: A quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel and equal must be a rectangle.
questions.explanation: Exercise Q5 answers 'No': such a quadrilateral is a parallelogram, which need not have right angles. So this cannot be used as a definition of a rectangle.

questions.topic: Rectangle Definitions and the Carpenter's Problem
questions.question: You have two sticks of equal length and a thread but no paper. How do you make an exact 90° angle?
options: Cross the sticks at their ends and run the thread around the two free ends
Lay the sticks side by side and stretch the thread diagonally across them
Cross the sticks at a quarter of their length and join the thread to the ends
Cross the sticks at their midpoints and run the thread around the four ends
questions.explanation: Equal sticks crossing at their midpoints are equal diagonals that bisect each other, so the thread forms a rectangle ACBD and every corner, e.g. ∠C, is 90°.

questions.topic: Rectangle Definitions and the Carpenter's Problem
questions.question: According to the chapter, who uses the equal-diagonals method to get rectangular shapes in practice?
options: Carpenters in Europe and house-builders in Mozambique
Carpenters in India and farmers in Kenya and Ghana
Boat-builders in Europe and farmers in Mozambique
Carpenters in Mozambique and farmers in Europe
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that carpenters in Europe use the method for rectangular frames and farmers in Mozambique use it to lay a rectangular base for houses.

questions.topic: Rectangle Definitions and the Carpenter's Problem
questions.question: Select the TWO things about the wooden strips that make the thread form a rectangle.
options: The strips are equal in length
The strips are joined at their midpoints
The strips cross at right angles
The strips are joined at their ends
One strip is twice as long as the other
questions.explanation: A rectangle needs equal diagonals that bisect each other. Crossing at right angles is only needed for a square; any angle works for a rectangle.

questions.question: Deduction 1 proves AC = BD in rectangle ABCD using which congruence?
options: ΔABC ≅ ΔBCD by SSS
ΔADC ≅ ΔDAB by SAS
ΔADC ≅ ΔDAB by AAS
ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOD by SAS
questions.explanation: AB = CD, ∠BAD = ∠CDA = 90° (the included angles) and AD is common, so SAS applies and AC = BD as corresponding parts.

questions.question: In Deduction 1, two of the matching facts are AB = CD and ∠BAD = ∠CDA = 90°. What is the third?
options: BD is common to both triangles
∠ABC = ∠DCB = 90° in both
AD is common to both triangles
AC is common to both triangles
questions.explanation: ΔADC and ΔDAB share side AD. AC and BD are the diagonals being compared — they cannot be assumed equal before the proof.

questions.question: Select the TWO facts used to show ΔADC ≅ ΔDAB in Deduction 1.
options: AB = CD
∠BAD = ∠CDA = 90°
AC = BD
OA = OC
questions.explanation: The SAS proof uses AB = CD, the right angles at A and D, and the common side AD. AC = BD is the conclusion, not a given; ∠1 = ∠2 and OA = OC belong to Deduction 2.

questions.question: Deduction 2 shows ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOD. Which condition and key fact does it use?
options: SAS, with the right angles at A and B
SSS, with OA = OC and OB = OD given
ASA, with the angles at A and C both 90°
AAS, with vertically opposite angles at O
questions.explanation: ∠AOB = ∠COD (vertically opposite), ∠1 = ∠2 (each 90° − ∠3) and AB = CD give AAS. OA = OC is what is being proved, so it cannot be a given.

questions.question: In Deduction 2, why is ∠1 (at A) equal to ∠2 (at C)?
options: Both equal 90° − ∠3, one from ∠B = 90° and one from ΔBCD's angle sum
Both are vertically opposite angles made by the crossing diagonals
Both are alternate angles made by diagonal BD with the parallel sides
Both are half of the 90° angle because the diagonals bisect the angles
questions.explanation: ∠3 + ∠1 = 90° because ∠B is a right angle, and ∠3 + ∠2 + 90° = 180° in ΔBCD gives ∠3 + ∠2 = 90°. So ∠1 = ∠2 = 90° − ∠3. The diagonals of a rectangle do not bisect its angles.

questions.question: What does Deduction 2 conclude about O, the intersection of the diagonals of a rectangle?
options: O divides each diagonal in the ratio 1 : 2
O is the midpoint of both diagonals
O is the midpoint of one diagonal only
O is equidistant from all four sides
questions.explanation: Since ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOD, OA = OC and OB = OD, so O is the midpoint of AC and of BD — the diagonals bisect each other.

questions.question: Equal diagonals bisect each other at 60°. In ΔAOB, where OA = OB and ∠AOB = 60°, what is each base angle a?
questions.explanation: a + a + 60 = 180 gives 2a = 120, so a = 60°. (ΔAOB is in fact equilateral.) 30° is the base angle of the neighbouring triangle with a 120° apex.

questions.question: In the same figure, ΔAOD has apex angle ∠AOD = 120° with OA = OD. What is each base angle b?
questions.explanation: b + b + 120 = 180 gives 2b = 60, so b = 30°. Each angle of the quadrilateral is then a + b = 60° + 30° = 90°.

questions.question: Equal diagonals bisect each other at an angle x. If a is a base angle of ΔAOB and b a base angle of ΔAOD, then:
options: a = 90° − x/2 and b = x/2
a = x/2 and b = 90° − x/2
a = 180° − x and b = x
a = 90° − x and b = 90° + x
questions.explanation: 2a + x = 180 gives a = 90 − x/2; 2b + (180 − x) = 180 gives b = x/2. Their sum a + b = 90°, so every angle of the quadrilateral is a right angle whatever x is.

questions.question: If two equal diagonals bisect each other, the quadrilateral is a rectangle only when the angle between the diagonals is 60° or 90°.
questions.explanation: The general argument with angle x shows every corner is (90° − x/2) + x/2 = 90° for ANY x. So the figure is a rectangle no matter what the angle between the diagonals is.

questions.question: Two 8 cm diagonals bisect each other and cross at 40°. What quadrilateral is formed?
options: Trapezium
Rectangle
Rhombus
Kite
questions.explanation: Equal diagonals that bisect each other always give a rectangle (exercise Q2 parts (i), (ii) and (iv)). Only when the angle is 90° does it become a square.

questions.question: Why are the sides AD and BC of rectangle ABCD parallel?
options: AD = BC — equal segments are always parallel to each other
∠A + ∠C = 180° — alternate angles on transversal AC
∠A + ∠B = 180° — co-interior angles on transversal AB
∠A = ∠C — opposite angles of the rectangle are equal
questions.explanation: AB is a transversal to AD and BC, and ∠A + ∠B = 90° + 90° = 180°. When interior angles on the same side of a transversal add to 180°, the lines are parallel.

questions.question: Which statement is Property 4 of a rectangle?
options: Diagonals are equal and perpendicular
Diagonals bisect each other at right angles
Diagonals bisect the angles of the rectangle
Diagonals are equal and bisect each other
questions.explanation: Property 4 states the diagonals of a rectangle are of equal length and bisect each other. Perpendicular diagonals and angle-bisecting diagonals are extra properties of a square.

questions.question: The diagonals of every rectangle bisect its angles.
questions.explanation: Only in a square (Property 5 of a square) do the diagonals bisect the corner angles into 45° halves. In a non-square rectangle a diagonal splits a 90° corner into unequal parts, e.g. 30° and 60°.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a property of every rectangle?
options: Diagonals meet at 90°
Diagonals are equal
Opposite sides parallel
All angles are 90°
questions.explanation: Perpendicular diagonals belong to squares and rhombuses, not to every rectangle. Equal diagonals, parallel opposite sides and right angles hold for all rectangles.

questions.question: Rectangle PQRS has diagonals meeting at O with ∠POS = 110°. What is ∠OQR?
questions.explanation: ∠QOR = ∠POS = 110° (vertically opposite). OQ = OR because the diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so ∠OQR = ∠ORQ = (180° − 110°) ÷ 2 = 35°.

questions.question: In rectangle ABCD, ∠ABD = 30°. What is ∠ADB?
questions.explanation: ΔABD is right-angled at A, so ∠ADB = 180° − 90° − 30° = 60°. The answer key lists ∠ADB = 60° and ∠BDC = 30°.

questions.question: In rectangle ABCD, ∠ABD = 30°. Which other angle also equals 30°?
options: ∠ADB
∠CAD
∠ACB
∠BDC
questions.explanation: AB ∥ DC with transversal BD, so ∠BDC = ∠ABD = 30° (alternate angles). ∠ADB, ∠CAD and ∠ACB are all 60° in the answer key.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements that are true for every rectangle.
options: Each diagonal splits it into two congruent triangles
The diagonals are of equal length
The diagonals cross at right angles
All four sides are of equal length
The diagonals bisect the corner angles
questions.explanation: Deduction 1 shows a diagonal creates congruent triangles and that the diagonals are equal. Right-angle crossing, equal sides and angle bisection are square-only properties.

questions.question: How does the chapter define a square?
options: All angles are 90° and all sides are equal
All angles are 90° and opposite sides are equal
All sides are equal and opposite angles are equal
Diagonals are equal and bisect each other
questions.explanation: A square is a quadrilateral with all angles 90° AND all sides equal — a special rectangle. The second option is a rectangle, the third a rhombus.

questions.question: In Deduction 5, ΔBOA ≅ ΔBOC in square ABCD is shown by which congruence condition?
options: ASA
SSS
SAS
AAS
questions.explanation: BA = BC (sides of the square), OA = OC (diagonals bisect each other) and BO is common — three sides, so SSS.

questions.question: Why must the diagonals of a square meet at 90°?
options: The diagonals are equal in length, and equal diagonals always cross at right angles
Each diagonal bisects a 90° corner, so the two diagonals must also meet at 90°
∠BOA = ∠BOC (congruent triangles) and they form a straight angle, so each is 90°
∠BOA and ∠BOC are vertically opposite angles, so each must be half of 180°
questions.explanation: ΔBOA ≅ ΔBOC gives ∠BOA = ∠BOC, and ∠BOA + ∠BOC = 180° (a straight angle), so each is 90°. Equal diagonals alone give only a rectangle.

questions.question: What angle does a diagonal of a square make with each side it meets?
questions.explanation: In ΔADC, ∠1 + ∠3 + 90° = 180° and AD = DC gives ∠1 = ∠3, so each is 45° — the diagonals bisect the square's right angles.

questions.question: To make the thread form a SQUARE, how must the carpenter join the two equal 8 cm strips?
options: At their midpoints and at right angles
At their midpoints at any angle
At their ends and at right angles
At their midpoints at 45° to each other
questions.explanation: Equal diagonals bisecting each other give a rectangle; adding the condition that they cross at 90° (Deduction 5) makes all sides equal, giving a square.

questions.question: Every property of a rectangle also holds for a square.
questions.explanation: A square is a special rectangle (all angles 90°), so all rectangle properties — equal opposite sides, parallel sides, equal bisecting diagonals — apply to it as well.

questions.question: A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other must be a square.
questions.explanation: Exercise Q11(i) is False: equal bisecting diagonals give a rectangle. For a square the diagonals must ALSO be perpendicular to each other.

questions.question: A quadrilateral has four equal sides and one angle of 90°. Is it a square? Why?
options: No — four equal sides only ever guarantee a rhombus, not a square
Yes — as a rhombus its adjacent angles sum to 180°, so all become 90°
No — the three remaining angles can still differ from 90° in a rhombus
Yes — one right angle in any quadrilateral forces all four to be 90°
questions.explanation: Four equal sides make a rhombus, where adjacent angles are supplementary and opposite angles equal. One 90° angle forces its neighbours to 90° and its opposite to 90°, so all four are right angles: a square.

questions.question: PL and AM are two perpendicular diameters of a circle with centre O. What figure is APML?
options: Rectangle
Kite
Square
Rhombus
questions.explanation: The diameters are equal, bisect each other at the centre O, and are perpendicular — equal diagonals bisecting at 90° give a square.

questions.question: CASE is a square and U, V, W, X are the midpoints of its sides. What quadrilateral is UVWX?
options: A rhombus that is not a square
A rectangle that is not a square
A kite that is not a rhombus
A square
questions.explanation: Each corner triangle is right-angled isosceles, so all four sides UV = VW = WX = XU (= x/√2) and the 45° + 45° angles leave 90° at each inner corner: a square.

questions.question: In exercise Q7 the square has side x. Using the right-angled corner triangle, UV² equals:
options: x²/4 + x²/4 = x²/2
x²/4 + x² = 5x²/4
x²/2 + x²/2 = x²
questions.explanation: CU = CV = x/2, so UV² = (x/2)² + (x/2)² = x²/4 + x²/4 = x²/2 by Pythagoras. Using a full side x for one leg, or multiplying the legs instead of squaring and adding, are the common slips.

questions.question: Which TWO properties belong to a square but NOT to every rectangle?
options: Diagonals meet at right angles
Diagonals bisect the corner angles
Diagonals are equal in length
Diagonals bisect each other
Opposite sides are parallel
questions.explanation: Square Properties 4 and 5 add perpendicular diagonals and angle-bisecting diagonals. Equal diagonals, mutual bisection and parallel sides hold for every rectangle.

questions.question: In the Venn diagram of squares and rectangles, how are the two regions drawn?
options: The two regions are drawn separately and do not touch
The square region lies entirely inside the rectangle region
The rectangle region lies entirely inside the square region
The two regions overlap only partly, like two linked rings
questions.explanation: Every square is a rectangle but not every rectangle is a square, so the set of squares sits completely inside the set of rectangles.

questions.question: The 'I am an Indian and I am a Malayali' cartoon illustrates which idea?
options: A single quadrilateral is allowed to carry only one name in geometry
Sets of shapes are always drawn as rectangles inside a Venn diagram
An object can belong to a smaller set and also to the bigger set containing it
Two different sets can never have a member in common at the same time
questions.explanation: Just as a Malayali is also an Indian, a square is also a rectangle — belonging to the smaller set does not stop it belonging to the larger one.

questions.question: Why is a rectangle also a parallelogram?
options: Its diagonals are equal, which is what the definition asks
Its angles are all 90°, which the definition requires
Its opposite sides are equal, which is what the definition asks
Its opposite sides are parallel, which is all the definition asks
questions.explanation: A parallelogram is defined only by having opposite sides parallel. A rectangle has this (Property 3), so it is a special parallelogram with all angles 90°.

questions.question: Which statement is NOT correct?
options: Every parallelogram is a rectangle
Every square is also a rhombus
Every rhombus is a parallelogram
Every square is a rectangle
questions.explanation: A parallelogram need not have right angles, so it is not necessarily a rectangle. The other three inclusions are all shown in the chapter's Venn diagrams.

questions.question: Which quadrilateral is both a kite and a parallelogram?
options: Kite only
Rhombus
Rectangle
Trapezium
questions.explanation: The answer key names the rhombus (and square): all sides equal gives adjacent pairs equal (kite) and opposite sides parallel (parallelogram).

questions.question: What is the correct relationship between kites and rhombuses?
options: Kites and rhombuses are exactly the same set of shapes
No kite can ever be a rhombus and no rhombus a kite
Every rhombus is a kite, but not every kite is a rhombus
Every kite is a rhombus, but not every rhombus is a kite
questions.explanation: A rhombus has all sides equal, so its adjacent pairs are equal — it is a kite. A kite with sides 6, 6, 9, 9 is not a rhombus.

questions.question: Which TWO of these shapes always have all four sides equal?
options: Rhombus
Square
Rectangle
Parallelogram
Kite
questions.explanation: A rhombus is defined by four equal sides and a square is a rhombus with right angles. Rectangles, parallelograms and kites can have unequal sides.

questions.question: Every rhombus is a parallelogram.
questions.explanation: Deduction 9 shows a diagonal of a rhombus makes equal alternate angles with the opposite sides, so both pairs are parallel — a rhombus is a parallelogram.

questions.question: A quadrilateral's diagonals bisect each other, are equal, AND are perpendicular. What is it?
options: A rectangle that is not a square
A rhombus that is not a square
A kite that is not a rhombus
A square
questions.explanation: Equal + bisecting gives a rectangle; bisecting + perpendicular gives a rhombus. Both together force a square.

questions.question: Exercise Q11(vii) says 'Isosceles trapeziums are parallelograms'. The key's verdict and reason?
options: False — the other pair of opposite sides need not be parallel
True — equal non-parallel sides make both pairs parallel
True — all trapeziums are parallelograms by definition
False — a trapezium never has any parallel sides
questions.explanation: An isosceles trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides; its equal sides are the non-parallel ones. So it is not a parallelogram.

questions.question: How does the chapter define a parallelogram?
options: A quadrilateral with two pairs of adjacent equal sides
A quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel
A quadrilateral whose opposite sides are equal
A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal
questions.explanation: A parallelogram is defined by parallel opposite sides. Equal opposite sides turn out to be a property (Deduction 7), not the definition; adjacent equal pairs describe a kite.

questions.question: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 30°. What is ∠D?
questions.explanation: AB ∥ CD with AD as transversal, so ∠A + ∠D = 180° (co-interior angles) and ∠D = 150°. The angle equal to 30° is the opposite one, ∠C.

questions.question: Why does ∠A + ∠D = 180° hold in parallelogram ABCD?
options: AD ∥ BC and AB is a transversal, so they are alternate angles
The diagonals bisect each other, splitting 360° into equal parts
∠A and ∠D are vertically opposite angles at the same vertex
AB ∥ CD and AD is a transversal, so they are co-interior angles
questions.explanation: ∠A and ∠D lie on the same side of transversal AD between the parallel lines AB and CD, so they are interior angles on the same side and add to 180°.

questions.question: In parallelogram PQRS, ∠P = 110°. What is ∠Q?
questions.explanation: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to 180°, so ∠Q = 180° − 110° = 70°. The answer key gives ∠Q = ∠S = 70° and ∠R = 110°.

questions.question: A parallelogram has one angle of 40°. What is the sum of the two angles adjacent to it?
questions.explanation: Each adjacent angle is 180° − 40° = 140°, so the two together make 280°. The key for exercise Q1(i) lists the angles as 40°, 140°, 40°, 140°.

questions.question: In a parallelogram, the opposite angles are equal and the adjacent angles add up to 180°.
questions.explanation: This is Property 3 of a parallelogram, proved in Deduction 6 using co-interior angles on the parallel sides.

questions.question: A quadrilateral in which the opposite angles are equal must be a parallelogram.
questions.explanation: Exercise Q11(v) is True. If ∠A = ∠C = x and ∠B = ∠D = y then 2x + 2y = 360°, so x + y = 180°; equal co-interior angle sums make both pairs of opposite sides parallel.

questions.question: When constructing the parallelogram with AB = 4 cm, AD = 5 cm and ∠A = 30°, what is Step 2?
options: Draw arcs of radius 5 cm from D and radius 4 cm from B; mark where they meet as C
Draw the diagonal from A and mark the point C exactly 9 cm away from A
Draw a line through D parallel to AB and a line through B parallel to AD; they meet at C
Draw a line through D perpendicular to AB and a line through B perpendicular to AD
questions.explanation: Parallel lines through D and B complete the parallelogram at C. Perpendiculars would build a rectangle; the arc radii are swapped (CD should be 4 cm and BC 5 cm).

questions.question: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 30°. Select the TWO correct statements.
questions.explanation: ∠B is adjacent to ∠A so ∠B = 150°; ∠C is opposite so ∠C = 30°. ∠D is also adjacent, so ∠D = 150°, not 30°.

questions.question: Deduction 7 shows ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB in a parallelogram using which condition?
options: SSS — three pairs of equal sides, with BD common to both
SAS — two sides and the included angle between them equal
ASA — using the two right angles at B and D with side BD
AAS — an opposite angle, an alternate angle, and common side BD
questions.explanation: The single-arc angles are equal (opposite angles of the parallelogram), the double-arc angles are alternate angles from AD ∥ BC, and BD is common — AAS. Sides cannot be assumed equal since that is what is being proved.

questions.question: Which statement is Property 1 of a parallelogram (about its sides)?
options: Opposite sides are equal
All sides are equal
Adjacent sides are equal
Opposite sides are perpendicular
questions.explanation: Property 1: the opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal. All sides equal is a rhombus; adjacent sides equal is a kite.

questions.question: A parallelogram has adjacent sides 4 cm and 5 cm. What are its other two sides?
options: 4.5 cm and 4.5 cm
4 cm and 5 cm
4 cm and 4 cm
5 cm and 5 cm
questions.explanation: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal, so the side opposite the 4 cm side is 4 cm and the side opposite the 5 cm side is 5 cm.

questions.question: The diagonals of a parallelogram are always equal in length.
questions.explanation: The chapter asks you to check your constructed parallelogram and notes that its diagonals need NOT be equal. Equal diagonals happen only in rectangles.

questions.question: In Deduction 8 (parallelogram EASY), ΔAOE ≅ ΔYOS is proved by which condition?
options: SAS
AAS
ASA
SSS
questions.explanation: AE = YS (opposite sides) is the included side between two pairs of equal alternate angles, so the condition is ASA.

questions.question: Which statement is Property 4 of a parallelogram (about its diagonals)?
options: They are equal in length
They meet at right angles
They bisect the angles
They bisect each other
questions.explanation: Deduction 8 proves OA = OY and OE = OS, so the diagonals bisect each other. They need not be equal, perpendicular or angle-bisecting.

questions.question: A quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other must be a parallelogram.
questions.explanation: Exercise Q11(iii) is True: with OA = OC, OB = OD and vertically opposite angles, SAS gives congruent triangles whose alternate angles show both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.

questions.question: Exercise Q9: what type of quadrilateral has both pairs of opposite sides equal, and why?
options: A parallelogram — SSS gives equal alternate angles, so both side-pairs are parallel
A rectangle — equal opposite sides force all four of the angles to be exactly 90°
A rhombus — having equal opposite sides means all four sides must be equal
A kite — equal opposite sides are the same thing as equal adjacent sides
questions.explanation: Drawing diagonal AC, ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA by SSS. The equal alternate angles give AB ∥ CD and BC ∥ AD, so the figure is a parallelogram (not necessarily a rectangle or rhombus).

questions.question: Is it wrong to write ΔABD ≅ ΔCBD instead of ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB in Deduction 7?
options: No — the order of letters never matters in congruence
Yes — vertex order must match: A↔C, B↔D, D↔B
No — both names list the same two triangles
Yes — B cannot appear in both triangle names
questions.explanation: In a congruence statement the letters must list corresponding vertices. A matches C, B matches D and D matches B, so ΔCDB is the correct order and ΔCBD would pair the wrong parts.

questions.question: Which TWO statements are true for the diagonals of EVERY parallelogram?
options: They bisect each other
Each diagonal splits it into two congruent triangles
They are equal in length
They are perpendicular
They bisect the angles
questions.explanation: Deduction 7 shows a diagonal makes two congruent triangles and Deduction 8 shows the diagonals bisect each other. Equality, perpendicularity and angle bisection need special parallelograms.

questions.question: How does the chapter define a rhombus?
options: Opposite sides are equal and parallel
Diagonals are equal and bisect each other
All sides have the same length
All angles have the same measure
questions.explanation: A rhombus is a quadrilateral in which all the sides have the same length. Equal angles would describe a rectangle.

questions.question: Rhombus ABCD has ∠A = 50° and diagonal BD makes four equal angles a with the sides. What is a?
questions.explanation: In ΔADB, a + a + 50° = 180°, so 2a = 130° and a = 65°. 130° is the obtuse angle of the rhombus, not the half-angle.

questions.question: Why is every rhombus a parallelogram (Deduction 9)?
options: A diagonal makes equal alternate angles with each pair of opposite sides, so they are parallel
All four of its sides are equal, and sides of equal length are always parallel to each other
Its diagonals are equal, and equal diagonals make opposite sides parallel
Its opposite angles are equal, and the definition of a parallelogram is about angles
questions.explanation: In rhombus GAME, ΔGAE ≅ ΔMAE gives a = b = c = d. Equal alternate angles on transversal AE show EM ∥ GA and GE ∥ AM, so GAME is a parallelogram.

questions.question: In rhombus GAME, ΔGAE ≅ ΔMAE is established by:
options: ASA (angles at A and E, side AE)
SSS (GA = MA, GE = ME, AE common)
SAS (GA = MA, ∠G = ∠M, AE common)
AAS (two angles and side AE)
questions.explanation: All sides of a rhombus are equal, so GA = MA and GE = ME, and AE is shared — three sides, SSS. ∠G = ∠M is a conclusion of this congruence, not a given.

questions.question: In Deduction 10, ∠GOE = ∠MOE and together they make a straight angle. What is each?
questions.explanation: ΔGEO ≅ ΔMEO gives ∠GOE = ∠MOE; since they add to 180°, each is 90°. This is Property 6: the diagonals of a rhombus meet at right angles.

questions.question: The diagonals of a rhombus are always equal in length.
questions.explanation: The chapter's rhombus properties say the diagonals bisect each other at 90° and bisect the angles — but not that they are equal. Only a square (a rhombus with right angles) has equal diagonals.

questions.question: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles and also bisect the angles of the rhombus.
questions.explanation: These are Properties 4, 5 and 6 of a rhombus: the diagonals bisect each other, bisect its angles, and intersect at 90°.

questions.question: In rhombus UVWX, diagonal VX makes an angle of 30° with side UV (∠XVU = 30°). What is ∠U?
questions.explanation: The diagonal bisects ∠V, so ∠UVW = 2 × 30° = 60°. Adjacent angles add to 180°, so ∠U = 180° − 60° = 120° (and ∠W = 120°).

questions.question: In rhombus AOIE, diagonal EO makes 20° with side EI (∠OEI = 20°). What is ∠A?
questions.explanation: ∠E = 2 × 20° = 40° because the diagonal bisects the angle. ∠A is adjacent to ∠E, so ∠A = 180° − 40° = 140°; the key also gives ∠I = 140°.

questions.question: Exercise Q11(iv): 'A quadrilateral whose diagonals are perpendicular must be a rhombus.' Verdict and reason?
options: True — perpendicular diagonals force all sides to be equal
False — a kite also has perpendicular diagonals
True — only a rhombus has perpendicular diagonals
False — a rectangle also has perpendicular diagonals
questions.explanation: The key says False: 'It may be a kite also.' A kite's diagonals are perpendicular but its four sides are not all equal.

questions.question: Which TWO properties hold for every rhombus but NOT for every parallelogram?
options: Diagonals meet at 90°
Diagonals bisect the angles
Diagonals bisect each other
Opposite angles are equal
Opposite sides are parallel
questions.explanation: Rhombus Properties 5 and 6 (angle-bisecting, perpendicular diagonals) are extra. Bisecting diagonals, equal opposite angles and parallel sides are shared with all parallelograms.

questions.question: The chapter labels a kite ABCD so that which sides are equal?
options: AB = BC = CD = DA
AB ∥ CD and BC = DA
AB = BC and CD = DA
AB = CD and BC = DA
questions.explanation: A kite has two pairs of equal ADJACENT sides: AB = BC and CD = DA. Equal opposite sides (AB = CD, BC = DA) describe a parallelogram.

questions.question: In the chapter's kite made from two 6-9-12 triangles, the 12 cm sides are glued together. What are the kite's side lengths?
questions.explanation: The shared 12 cm side becomes the diagonal BD and disappears from the boundary, leaving 6 cm and 9 cm from each triangle — adjacent pairs 6, 6 and 9, 9.

questions.question: Kite Property 1 says diagonal BD does what to the other diagonal AC?
options: Bisects AC and is perpendicular to it
Is equal to AC and bisects it
Is bisected by AC and is perpendicular to it
Is parallel to AC and equal to it
questions.explanation: Property 1(ii): BD bisects AC (AO = OC) and is perpendicular to it. BD itself is generally not bisected and the diagonals are not equal.

questions.question: In kite ABCD (AB = BC, CD = DA), which angles does the diagonal BD bisect?
options: All four angles of the kite
∠ABC and ∠ADC
∠BAD and ∠BCD
∠ABC and ∠BAD
questions.explanation: BD joins the two vertices where the equal sides meet, so it bisects ∠ABC and ∠ADC. The other two angles are not bisected (unless the kite is a rhombus).

questions.question: To prove the kite property, which pair of triangles does the chapter's hint ask you to compare?
options: ΔABC and ΔADC
ΔAOB and ΔAOD
ΔAOB and ΔCOB
ΔAOD and ΔCOB
questions.explanation: The hint is 'Is ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOB?' — these triangles share BO, have AB = CB, and lie on either side of diagonal BD, giving AO = OC and right angles at O.

questions.question: How does the answer key construct a kite with diagonals 6 cm and 8 cm?
options: Draw PQ = 6 cm, draw a line through its midpoint at 60°, place R and S so RS = 8 cm
Draw PQ = 6 cm and RS = 8 cm so that they cross at their midpoints at any angle
Draw PQ = 6 cm, then draw RS = 8 cm parallel to PQ at a distance of 3 cm from it
Draw PQ = 6 cm, draw its perpendicular bisector, place R and S on it so RS = 8 cm
questions.explanation: A kite's diagonals are perpendicular and one bisects the other. So RS lies on the perpendicular bisector of PQ with RS = 8 cm (RS itself need not be bisected).

questions.question: In a kite, both diagonals bisect each other.
questions.explanation: Only one diagonal is bisected: BD bisects AC (AO = OC), but AC does not in general bisect BD. Mutual bisection would make it a parallelogram.

questions.question: The chapter summary describes a kite as a quadrilateral with two non-overlapping adjacent pairs of sides of the same length.
questions.explanation: The summary says exactly this — 'two non-overlapping adjacent pairs of sides having the same length', matching AB = BC and CD = DA.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT necessarily true for a kite?
options: Opposite sides are parallel
One diagonal bisects the other
The diagonals are perpendicular
Two pairs of adjacent sides are equal
questions.explanation: A kite has no parallel sides in general — the 6-6-9-9 kite has none. Perpendicular diagonals, one bisecting the other, and equal adjacent pairs are its defining features.

questions.question: Select the TWO true statements about kite ABCD with AB = BC and CD = DA.
options: BD is perpendicular to AC
BD bisects AC
AC bisects BD
AB is parallel to CD
BD is equal to AC
questions.explanation: Property 1: BD bisects AC and is perpendicular to it. AC does not bisect BD, the diagonals are not equal, and a kite has no parallel sides in general.

questions.question: How does the chapter define a trapezium?
options: Two pairs of equal adjacent sides
At least one pair of parallel opposite sides
Exactly two pairs of parallel opposite sides
No pair of parallel sides at all
questions.explanation: A trapezium relaxes the parallelogram condition: it needs AT LEAST one pair of parallel opposite sides.

questions.question: In trapezium PQRS with PQ ∥ SR, which angle relations does Property 1 give?
options: ∠S = ∠P and ∠R = ∠Q
questions.explanation: PS and QR are transversals to the parallel sides PQ and SR, so the co-interior angles ∠S + ∠P and ∠R + ∠Q each add to 180°.

questions.question: Trapezium PQRS has PQ ∥ RS, ∠P = 135° and ∠Q = 105°. What is ∠R?
questions.explanation: ∠R + ∠Q = 180° (co-interior), so ∠R = 180° − 105° = 75°. 45° is ∠S, the angle paired with ∠P.

questions.question: Trapezium PQRS has PQ ∥ RS, ∠P = 135° and ∠Q = 105°. What is ∠S?
What is an isosceles trapezium?
options: A trapezium whose diagonals are perpendicular
A trapezium whose non-parallel sides are equal
A trapezium whose parallel sides are equal
A trapezium with two right angles at one base
questions.explanation: When the two non-parallel sides have the same length, the trapezium is called isosceles. Equal parallel sides would make it a parallelogram.

questions.question: ABCD is an isosceles trapezium with AD = BC and ∠D = 100°. What is ∠A?
questions.explanation: ∠A + ∠D = 180° (co-interior), so ∠A = 80°. By Property 2 the angles opposite the equal sides are equal, so ∠B = ∠A = 80° too.

questions.question: To prove ∠U = ∠V in isosceles trapezium UVWX, perpendiculars XY and WZ are dropped to UV. Why is XWZY a rectangle?
options: XY = WZ, and any quadrilateral with two equal opposite sides is a rectangle
XW = YZ, and equal opposite sides are enough to make a rectangle
The diagonals of XWZY are equal, which is the chapter's definition of a rectangle
XW ∥ YZ and XY, WZ are transversals, so co-interior angles make a = b = 90°
questions.explanation: Since XW ∥ UV, a = 180° − ∠XYZ = 90° and b = 180° − ∠WZY = 90°. With the two right angles at Y and Z, all four angles are 90°, so XWZY is a rectangle.

questions.question: What is Property 2 of an isosceles trapezium?
options: The angles opposite the equal sides are equal
The diagonals bisect each other at their midpoints
The equal sides are parallel to each other
All four of its angles are equal to each other
questions.explanation: ΔUXY ≅ ΔVWZ gives ∠U = ∠V: in an isosceles trapezium the angles opposite to the equal sides are equal.

questions.question: In an isosceles trapezium, the two parallel sides must be of equal length.
questions.explanation: It is the NON-parallel sides that are equal. If the parallel sides were also equal the figure would be a parallelogram, not a trapezium with just one parallel pair.

questions.question: Trapezium PQRS has PQ ∥ SR with ∠P = 135° and ∠Q = 105°. What is ∠R + ∠S?
questions.explanation: The four angles total 360°, so ∠R + ∠S = 360° − (135° + 105°) = 120°. Indeed ∠R = 75° and ∠S = 45°.

questions.question: In trapezium PQRS with PQ ∥ SR, which TWO angle pairs must add up to 180°?
options: ∠P and ∠S
∠Q and ∠R
∠P and ∠Q
∠P and ∠R
∠S and ∠R
questions.explanation: The non-parallel sides PS and QR act as transversals, so ∠P + ∠S = 180° and ∠Q + ∠R = 180°. Angles along a parallel side (∠P, ∠Q) need not be supplementary.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what is a conjecture?
options: A statement that has been shown false by one example
A measurement taken from several real-world shapes
A statement we are highly confident about but have not yet proved
A statement that has been proved true by deduction
questions.explanation: Observations and measurements let us form a conjecture — a statement we feel sure about but cannot yet be certain always holds. Only a proof settles it.

questions.question: Why is measuring many rectangles NOT enough to be sure their diagonals always bisect each other?
options: Rulers and protractors are never accurate enough to measure a diagonal exactly
Rectangles drawn on paper are never exactly the same as geometric rectangles
The property has been checked to hold only for the first 1000 rectangles drawn
Measurements only support a conjecture; a proof is needed to be sure for all cases
questions.explanation: The chapter asks: can we be sure the 1000th rectangle also has the property? Only by justifying (proving) the statement, as in Deduction 2, can we be certain.

questions.question: Is it wrong to write ΔBAD ≅ ΔCDB instead of ΔBAD ≅ ΔDCB in Deduction 4?
options: Yes — the vertex order must match: B↔D, A↔C, D↔B
No — both names list the same three vertices
Yes — a triangle name must always start with A
No — congruence does not depend on the order of letters
questions.explanation: Congruence statements pair corresponding vertices in order. B corresponds to D, A to C and D to B, so ΔDCB is correct; ΔCDB would claim BA = CD's wrong partner.

questions.question: Why can't AO = CO, ∠AOB = ∠COD and AD = CB be used to prove ΔAOD ≅ ΔCOB?
options: Three equal parts can never be enough to prove two triangles congruent
∠AOB is not an angle of ΔAOD; the angle needed is ∠AOD = ∠COB
AO = CO has not been proved and is not true in a rectangle
AD = CB is a property that has not yet been proved for rectangles
questions.explanation: The angle must belong to the triangles being compared. ∠AOB lies in ΔAOB, not ΔAOD; the matching vertically opposite angles for these triangles are ∠AOD and ∠COB.

questions.question: Deduction 4 (all angles 90° ⇒ opposite sides equal) uses which congruence condition for ΔBAD ≅ ΔDCB?
options: SSS
ASA
AAS
SAS
questions.explanation: Right angles at A and C, ∠1 = ∠2 (both 90° − ∠3) and the common side BD give two angles and a non-included side: AAS, just as in Deduction 2.

questions.question: The chapter uses the SAS condition in Deduction 1 and the SSS condition in Deduction 5.
questions.explanation: Deduction 1 (equal diagonals of a rectangle) uses SAS with the right angles included; Deduction 5 (square diagonals at 90°) uses SSS on ΔBOA and ΔBOC.

questions.question: In Deduction 2, the 'blue' angles ∠AOB and ∠COD are equal because they are:
options: Alternate interior angles
Co-interior (allied) angles
Corresponding angles
Vertically opposite angles
questions.explanation: The diagonals cross at O, so ∠AOB and ∠COD are vertically opposite and therefore equal. Alternate angles need a transversal across parallel lines.

questions.question: Both Deduction 2 (rectangle) and Deduction 8 (parallelogram) prove the diagonals bisect each other. What does the parallelogram proof rely on?
options: Alternate angles from parallel sides (ASA)
Right angles at the vertices (AAS)
Equal diagonals of the parallelogram (SSS)
Perpendicular diagonals (SAS)
questions.explanation: A parallelogram has no right angles to use, so Deduction 8 uses the two pairs of alternate angles made by the diagonals with the parallel sides, plus AE = YS, giving ASA.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements that the chapter PROVES (not just conjectures).
options: Diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other
Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal
Diagonals of a parallelogram are always equal
Diagonals of a kite bisect each other
questions.explanation: Deduction 2 proves the first and Deduction 6 the second. The other two are false: parallelogram diagonals need not be equal, and in a kite only one diagonal is bisected.

questions.question: To draw a quadrilateral with equal 8 cm diagonals bisecting at 30°, you draw AB = 8 cm, midpoint O and a line at 30° through O. Where do C and D go?
options: 4 cm from A and B respectively
4 cm from O on either side
8 cm from O on either side
2 cm from O on either side
questions.explanation: The second diagonal must also be 8 cm and be bisected at O, so OC = OD = 4 cm. Then ADBC is the required quadrilateral (a rectangle).

questions.question: For a parallelogram with diagonals 7 cm and 5 cm meeting at 140°, the key draws AB = 7 cm with midpoint O. What radius is used for the arcs locating C and D?
options: 5 cm
7 cm
2.5 cm
3.5 cm
questions.explanation: The 5 cm diagonal is bisected at O, so OC = OD = 2.5 cm. 3.5 cm is half of the 7 cm diagonal already drawn.

questions.question: Which steps construct a rhombus with diagonals 4 cm and 5 cm?
options: Draw AB = 5 cm, a line at 60° through midpoint O, mark C and D 2 cm from O
Draw AB = 5 cm, its perpendicular through midpoint O, mark C and D 4 cm from O
Draw AB = 4 cm, its perpendicular through midpoint O, mark C and D 5 cm from O
Draw AB = 5 cm, its perpendicular through midpoint O, mark C and D 2 cm from O
questions.explanation: Rhombus diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so the 4 cm diagonal is drawn perpendicular to AB with OC = OD = 2 cm. Marking 4 cm from O would give an 8 cm diagonal.

questions.question: How do you construct a square with a 6 cm diagonal without a protractor?
options: Draw AB = 6 cm, construct its perpendicular bisector with a compass, mark C and D 3 cm from O
Draw AB = 6 cm, draw any line through its midpoint O, mark C and D 3 cm from O
Draw AB = 6 cm, construct its perpendicular bisector with a compass, mark C and D 6 cm from O
Draw AB = 3 cm, construct its perpendicular bisector with a compass, mark C and D 3 cm from O
questions.explanation: A square's diagonals are equal and bisect each other at 90°. The compass-drawn perpendicular bisector replaces the protractor, and OC = OD = 3 cm makes CD = 6 cm = AB.

questions.question: When building shapes from their diagonals, what separates a rhombus from a general parallelogram?
options: Parallelogram diagonals must bisect each other; rhombus diagonals need not bisect
Rhombus diagonals must be perpendicular; parallelogram diagonals may meet at any angle
Rhombus diagonals must be equal; parallelogram diagonals need not be equal at all
Parallelogram diagonals must be perpendicular; rhombus diagonals may meet at any angle
questions.explanation: Both have diagonals that bisect each other (Property 4). The rhombus adds Property 6 — the diagonals meet at 90° — which is why the parallelogram in exercise Q2 could use 140°.

questions.question: On a geoboard, two rubber bands of EQUAL length are placed perpendicular to each other, crossing at their midpoints, as diagonals. Joining the ends gives a:
options: Rhombus
Kite
Square
Rectangle
questions.explanation: Equal diagonals that bisect each other give a rectangle; being perpendicular as well makes all sides equal, so the figure is a square.

questions.question: In the geoboard activity, ONE of the two equal perpendicular diagonals is extended by 2 cm at both ends. What is the new quadrilateral?
options: Rectangle — diagonals are still equal and bisect each other
Kite — only one diagonal is now bisected by the other
Square — extending both ends equally keeps it a square
Rhombus — diagonals still bisect at 90° but are no longer equal
questions.explanation: Extending both ends by the same 2 cm keeps the midpoint fixed, so the diagonals still bisect each other at right angles, but one is now longer: a rhombus, not a square.

questions.question: Which TWO conditions on the diagonals are needed to guarantee a rectangle?
options: They are equal in length
They bisect each other
They are perpendicular to each other
They bisect the angles
They meet at 60°
questions.explanation: The Carpenter's Problem shows equal diagonals that bisect each other always form a rectangle, at any angle. Perpendicularity would additionally make it a square.

questions.question: Two cardboard equilateral triangles with 8 cm sides are joined along a side. What do you get?
options: A rhombus with all sides 8 cm
A square with all sides 8 cm
A rectangle with sides 8 cm and 16 cm
A trapezium with three sides of 8 cm
questions.explanation: The shared side disappears, leaving four sides of 8 cm each — a rhombus. It is not a square because its angles are 60° and 120°, not 90°.

questions.question: What are the angles of the quadrilateral made by joining two equilateral triangles with 4 cm sides?
questions.explanation: Each triangle angle is 60°. Two corners keep a single 60°, while the two corners where triangles meet have 60° + 60° = 120°. Check: 60 + 120 + 60 + 120 = 360.

questions.question: Two isosceles triangles with sides 8, 8, 6 cm are joined along their 6 cm sides. What quadrilateral results?
options: Parallelogram (sides 8, 6, 8, 6 cm)
Isosceles trapezium (sides 8, 6, 8, 6 cm)
Rhombus (all sides 8 cm)
Kite (sides 8, 8, 6, 6 cm)
questions.explanation: Gluing the 6 cm sides hides them, so the boundary is the four 8 cm sides — a rhombus. Joining along an 8 cm side instead would leave 6 cm sides on the boundary.

questions.question: Two isosceles 8-8-6 triangles are joined along an 8 cm side as mirror images of each other. What quadrilateral results?
options: Rhombus with all sides 8 cm
Rectangle with sides 8 cm and 6 cm
Square with all sides 6 cm
Kite with sides 8, 8, 6, 6 cm
questions.explanation: The glued 8 cm side becomes a diagonal. Each triangle contributes a free 8 cm and 6 cm side; mirroring puts the two 8 cm sides together at one end and the two 6 cm sides at the other — a kite.

questions.question: Two scalene triangles with sides 6, 9, 12 cm are joined along their 12 cm sides as mirror images. The result is a:
options: Kite
Rhombus
Rectangle
Square
questions.explanation: The chapter shows this exact join: adjacent sides come out equal (6, 6 and 9, 9), which is the definition of a kite. A rhombus would need all four sides equal.

questions.question: Joining two congruent equilateral triangles along a side always gives a rhombus.
questions.explanation: All four remaining sides equal the triangle's side, so the figure is a rhombus (with angles 60° and 120°). The chapter's 8 cm example shows this.

questions.question: Joining two congruent scalene triangles along a common side always gives a kite.
questions.explanation: Only a mirror-image join gives a kite. Rotating one triangle 180° about the midpoint of the shared side gives a parallelogram instead — the chapter asks for the 'different ways' precisely because the result varies.

questions.question: Which TWO quadrilaterals can be made by joining two congruent 8-8-6 isosceles triangles along a full side?
options: Rhombus
Kite
Square
Rectangle
questions.explanation: Joining along the 6 cm sides gives a rhombus; joining along an 8 cm side as mirror images gives a kite. A square or rectangle would need 90° angles, which an 8-8-6 triangle does not supply.
